chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Industry or Classification Unit Information
chunks.text:
Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production – CU Name of Industry or #763025 Classification Unit This classification unit description provides an overview of the Description of typical classification unit for general guidance only. Firms are classified work conducted in this based on this, our classification policies, Rate and Industry or Classification List, and other relevant classification unit Classification Unit descriptions. The items listed below are examples only; they are intended to be illustrative (not exhaustive). Every example may not apply to every firm in the classification unit. Here are some examples of goods that firms in this classification unit produce:
• Commercials
• Educational programs
• Music videos
• Videos
• Documentaries
• Motion pictures
• Television programs
• Movies of the week Here are some examples of facilities covered by this classification unit:
• Film sets (outdoors or indoors)
• Film studio Firms in this classification unit may engage in additional activities that support their business undertaking. These activities include finance and administrative support and may also include:
• Casting
• Set decoration
• Set construction

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Does this industry or classification unit contain hazards relating to confined space entry?
chunks.text: Not a typical hazard for this industry.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Does this industry or classification unit contain hazards relating to working from heights?
chunks.text: Yes. Working from heights is usually conducted by riggers who set up the rigging for camera/lighting. Electricians also work on height to maintain the lighting. They usually use scissor lifts to get access to the beams of the studio. A boom lift is used for outdoor setting up. Much of the stunt work performed by actors involves planned falls from heights. Performance work (trapeze, balcony, platform, etc.) is often conducted at heights. Camera crews work at heights typically from powered elevating work platforms.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Does this industry or classification unit contain hazards relating to machine safeguarding?
chunks.text: Yes. The construction department uses a lot of woodworking machines. Table saws are the most common machines. Other common equipment are hand grinders, heated and hard wire cutting tools (cut Styrofoam) and drills. Much of the equipment used in set design and construction is typical of what is found in a traditional cabinet/carpentry shop.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Does this industry or classification unit contain hazards relating to machine and equipment lockout?
chunks.text: Yes. As mentioned earlier, woodworking machines need to be locked out. In addition, some tools such as foam cutting wires and paint sprays need to be locked out for maintenance. Lighting equipment (generators), compressors, mobile equipment all may require de- energization and lockout for maintenance purposes.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Does this industry or classification unit contain hazards requiring respiratory programs?
chunks.text: Yes. Work activities that generate significant airborne hazards include woodworking, spray painting, foam cutting and welding/fabricating. Sometimes significant amount of theatrical fog might be used in shooting which would require respiratory protection.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Does this industry or classification unit require Exposure Control Plans (ECPs)?
chunks.text:
Yes. Activities that require ECPs include:
• Spraying painting (including adhesives)
• Using of crystalline silica-based surface dusting (to make the surface look old)
• Welding/Fabricating

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Industry or Classification Unit Hazards
chunks.text:
• Woodworking
• Carbon monoxide exposure control plan when there are sources of emission such as operating a vehicle inside the building

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Does this industry or classification unit contain hazards relating to mobile equipment and/or the requirement for roll-over protection (ROPs)?
chunks.text: Yes. Most sites have forklift, either propane or electric. Other equipment include scissor lift, boom lift or vehicles (car or motorcycle) used for shooting. One particular vehicle worth paying special attention is the first aid truck where first air treatment is provided. The injured worker would be lifted up to the deck of the truck. Other hazards include the loading/unloading of production equipment via the use of powered tailgates fitted to delivery trucks, and to ensure mobile equipment wheels are adequately chalked to prevent run-a-way vehicle hazard.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Does this industry or classification unit contain hazards of musculoskeletal injuries (MSI)?
chunks.text: Yes. Workers usually work 12 hour shift. A lot of job categories have higher MSI risk, such as camera, rigging and construction. The work involves large amounts of bending, twisting, lifting motions (i.e., camera cables, rigging materials, electrical equipment, etc.)

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Does this industry or classification unit contain hazards of working alone?
chunks.text: While not a typical hazard there can be situations where a worker is required to work alone, such as security personnel during after hours, Location Assistants scouting new areas, workers travelling from one film location to another during their work shift, to name a few.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Does this industry or classification unit contain hazards relating to contractor safety?
chunks.text: Yes. Cleaning crew may be present on site.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Does this industry or classification unit contain hazards relating to Toxic Process Gases?
chunks.text: This is not a typical hazard for this classification unit unless crews are working/shooting in an area where toxic process gases may be present (e.g., ice arena, swimming pool, pulp/paper mill, etc.)

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Stacking, storing, and housekeeping
chunks.text: The issues with hazards relating to stacking, storing, and housekeeping are unsafe stacking and storing of materials, overloading of racking crowding of work areas. The yard of a film set may be crowded and a lot of construction materials may be stacked. Inside trucks you may see stacking materials too.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Racking
chunks.text: The issues with hazards relating to racking are unknown rated capacity, damaged racking, and mismatched components. Racking may be used to store materials in the yard or inside trucks.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Trailers
chunks.text: The issues with hazards relating to trailers are no chocking/securement of trailer to prevent trailer creep, damaged trailers and “unzipping”, support of trailer to prevent upending. This industry uses a lot trailers either parked near the set studio or outdoor shooting locations.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Safe access and egress on loading docks and throughout warehouse
chunks.text: Safe access and egress to/from the set building is an issue because it is usually crowded around the safe access/egress and the signs may not be obvious.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Pedestrian separation from mobile equipment
chunks.text: The issue with hazards relating to pedestrian separation from mobile equipment are unmarked walkways, and lack of coordination between mobile equipment and pedestrians This could be inside the set building and in the yard. One need to be carefully looking for the marks as a pedestrian.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: General lighting conditions
chunks.text: The issue with hazards relating to general lighting conditions are ensuring minimum standards are maintained and lack of emergency lighting. The lighting for an active shooting stage can be very dim.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.section: Prevention Officer Personal Safety While On-Site
chunks.heading: Prevention Officer Personal Safety While On-Site
chunks.text:
Does this industry or classification unit require specific Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) the Prevention Officer must don while they are on-site?
• High visibility apparel
• Safety footwear
• Additional PPE, if there are other specifically identified hazards, such as respirator and safety glasses Does this industry or classification unit require the Prevention Officer to use air monitoring equipment while they are on-site? Maybe. For certain hygiene hazard, such as fog and wood dust, air monitoring equipment may be used to understand the magnitude of exposures. Does this industry or classification unit require the Prevention Officer to protect themselves against dogs while they are on-site? Maybe. Some sets allow workers to bring pets to work; some sets use large animals. Do not touch any animals and always stay with your escort. Animals of all kinds may be present if required to be included in the filming activity.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Risk Assessment Process
chunks.text: Does this industry or classification unit require a specific Risk Assessment Process the Prevention Officer must/should follow while they are conducting an inspection? Yes. Before conducting an inspection, always find the site office and talk to the production manager first. Ask for a copy of the Call Sheet to assist in identifying the key personnel on site or responsible for worker safety. Understand what the show is about – such as if it involves explosives, animals, children, etc. Also assess what kinds of hazards could be present – if overhead operation is in place; if theatrical fog is used; if flammable adhesive is used; if a spray booth has been set up; if vehicles are operated inside the building; etc. The risk levels can be quite different based on the activities. Follow proper safe work procedures and use proper PPE if the hazards are present. Be alert for a sounding buzzer or flashing red light on set which indicates the cameras are rolling – during these times limit your conversation with workers (speak quietly or not at all) until the light is off.

chunks.sheetTitle: Motion Picture, Commercial, or Television Production (CU 763025)
chunks.heading: Personal Protective Equipment (for Workers)
chunks.text:
Does this industry or classification unit require specific Personal Protective Equipment that the workers must don while they carry out their job functions?
• High visibility apparel (in the yard)
• Safety footwear
• Gloves (in construction)
• Safety glasses (in construction)
• Ty-vek suits and respirator (spray painting)
• Appropriate clothing
• Headgear (if working under overhead operations)
